title: FLOPs
subtitle: Topic: FLOPs · Subject: Efficient and Edge AI · Seven questions, concept-specific SVG explanations and a PyTorch profiling example.

FLOPs · EFFICIENT AND EDGE AI

Count computation. Measure real performance.

Learn what operation counts reveal—and what edge latency, memory, energy and hardware tests still need to prove.

questions.stem: What are FLOPs in Machine Learning, and how do they differ from FLOP/s when estimating the computational cost of an AI model?
options: FLOPs count floating-point operations required for one model pass, while FLOP/s describes the same total divided by the number of model parameters, making it a measure of computational work per stored weight.

FLOPs count floating-point arithmetic operations needed for a specified model computation, such as one forward pass. FLOP/s measures how many such operations hardware executes per second, describing a rate rather than a workload.

FLOPs estimate floating-point work from an operation's tensor shapes, while FLOP/s gives the number of operations in one training epoch. Both therefore describe fixed model workloads rather than a device's execution speed.

FLOPs measure floating-point arithmetic completed per second, while FLOP/s reports how many operations a model requires for one prediction. The two units are interchangeable after the batch size is specified.
questions.explanation: Explanation: FLOPs are a count of floating-point operations for a defined workload. A model might require 200 million FLOPs for one image, while FLOP/s tells us how quickly a device performs operations. That rate depends on hardware and software efficiency. For example, two smart cameras can run the same model with the same estimated FLOPs but finish at different speeds. Always state the input shape, batch size, and whether you counted inference or training, since the workload can change.

questions.stem: What is a multiply-accumulate operation (MAC), how is it related to FLOPs, and why can reported model operation counts differ between tools?
options: A MAC multiplies values and adds the result to an accumulator, so counting it as one FLOP is mandatory across profilers. Differences between reported models must therefore come only from rounding their final totals.

A MAC means multiplying one matrix by another without additions, and therefore counts as exactly two floating-point operations for every matrix element. Profilers differ mainly in how they count model parameters.

A MAC performs a multiplication and accumulation, but it always requires three FLOPs because accessing a weight is included as arithmetic. Profiling differences disappear if every tool uses the same batch size.

A MAC multiplies values and adds the product into an accumulator. Under a common convention it represents roughly two FLOPs, but tools may report MACs directly or use different counting rules for fused and other operations.
questions.explanation: Explanation: A multiply-accumulate performs multiplication followed by addition into a running result. Many neural-network estimates count that as two floating-point operations; some reports present MACs instead. One convolution may therefore be described as 5 million MACs or approximately 10 million FLOPs. The conversion is not enough to reconcile every profiler: bias additions, activation functions, fused kernels, and unsupported operations can be counted differently. When comparing edge models, check what a tool actually includes, rather than trusting a headline number alone.

questions.stem: How do input resolution, kernel size, input channels, output channels, and groups affect the FLOPs of a convolutional neural network layer?
options: Convolution FLOPs scale with output height and width, output channels, input channels per group, and kernel area. Under the two-FLOPs-per-MAC convention, the main convolution cost is approximately twice their product and batch size.

Convolution FLOPs grow with image resolution and output channels, but the number of input channels does not affect arithmetic once the kernel size is chosen. Grouping changes memory layout without reducing multiplications.

Convolution FLOPs scale with the total stored weights alone, so doubling output height and width does not change the work needed for one image. Batch size and feature-map dimensions influence only memory.

Convolution FLOPs grow with input and output channels and kernel area, but grouping always multiplies arithmetic by the group count. Doubling image height and width approximately doubles, rather than quadruples, spatial work.
questions.explanation: Explanation: A convolution applies a kernel at many output positions. For a conventional 2D convolution, MACs are approximately batch × output height × output width × output channels × input channels per group × kernel height × kernel width. Doubling both output dimensions usually creates about four times as many positions. For example, an edge camera processing higher-resolution frames needs more convolution work even when its model weights stay unchanged. The usual FLOP estimate multiplies the MAC count by two; bias and activation work may be reported separately.

questions.stem: Why does a neural network with fewer FLOPs not always achieve lower latency or energy consumption on an edge device?
options: FLOPs estimate arithmetic work, but latency is determined mainly by how many parameters a model stores. If a lower-FLOP model has fewer weights, it must run faster on every supported edge accelerator.

FLOPs omit some memory activity and hardware overhead, but models with identical FLOPs always have equivalent latency when batch size matches. Differences among phones mainly affect accuracy rather than speed or energy.

FLOPs estimate arithmetic work but omit memory transfers, kernel overhead, parallel utilization, and accelerator support. A lower-FLOP model can still run slower or use more energy, so engineers must benchmark target hardware and realistic inputs.

FLOPs approximate computations rather than measured time, but edge latency depends only on peak device FLOP/s. Using this advertised rate gives reliable response times without profiling memory behavior or individual operators.
questions.explanation: Explanation: FLOPs are a useful arithmetic estimate, not a stopwatch or battery meter. On a small device, loading weights, moving tensors, launching kernels, and using unsupported operators can dominate execution. For example, a compact vision network with many tiny layers may have fewer FLOPs yet run slower than a network with larger, efficiently fused layers. Accelerator type and batch size also matter. Benchmark the actual edge device, and measure p95 latency and power rather than assuming a smaller operation count guarantees a better experience.

questions.stem: How can a developer estimate a model's inference FLOPs with PyTorch, and what limitations should they consider when interpreting profiler results?
options: Run inference with torch.profiler and with_flops enabled, then treat its summed estimates as a complete count of every operator and device transfer. The result directly predicts measured latency without requiring hardware benchmarks.

Run representative inference inputs through torch.profiler with with_flops enabled, inspect the per-operation estimates, and compare shapes and workload settings consistently. The reported FLOPs cover supported operators, not necessarily every activation or end-to-end runtime cost.

Enable with_flops while running training on arbitrary random input shapes, then use the recorded number as the fixed FLOPs per inference for every image size and batch. Profiler coverage does not depend on operator type.

Profile a model once with with_flops enabled and compare its result against the number of trainable parameters. These two values should match for common layers, allowing unsupported operations and input shapes to be ignored.
questions.explanation: Explanation: PyTorch's profiler can estimate FLOPs for supported operations, including matrix multiplication and 2D convolution, when `with_flops=True`. Run the actual inference shape and inspect the operator table, as in the short Python example below. For example, a wildlife-camera classifier may be profiled at its deployed image size rather than a small training thumbnail. Some activations and other operations are not included in the FLOP estimate, so also measure elapsed time and memory on the target hardware. FLOPs are not automatically a complete model benchmark.

05 · VISUAL LESSON

Profile a representative forward pass

PyTorch · profile inference FLOPs12 lines
01 import torch
02 from torch import nn
03 from torch.profiler import profile, ProfilerActivity
04 model = nn.Conv2d(16, 32, 3, padding=1).eval()
05 x = torch.randn(1, 16, 32, 32)
06 with torch.no_grad():
07     with profile(
08         activities=[ProfilerActivity.CPU],
09         with_flops=True
10     ) as report:
11         model(x)
12 print(report.key_averages().table(sort_by="flops", row_limit=5))

CPU example: run with PyTorch installed. with_flops=True estimates selected operators; it does not benchmark edge latency or count every model operation.

PyTorch with_flops estimates selected operators, including matrix multiplication and Conv2d.

questions.stem: How can pruning, depthwise-separable convolutions, quantization, and knowledge distillation change compute demands for Efficient and Edge AI?
options: Structured pruning removes channels and depthwise-separable convolution splits convolution work, but both preserve exactly the same arithmetic count. Distillation and quantization help only by reducing the number of training examples needed.

Pruning and distillation can build smaller networks, while quantization uses lower precision, but quantizing FP32 weights to INT8 always divides a model's FLOP count and measured inference time by four on every device.

Depthwise convolution reduces channel mixing work and pruning may shrink layers, but knowledge distillation keeps the original large teacher model for inference. Quantization changes how many neurons the network contains rather than numeric precision.

Structured pruning can remove channels or layers, depthwise-separable convolution reduces many convolution MACs, and distillation trains a smaller student. Quantization lowers precision and can speed supported hardware, but its integer operations are not simply floating-point FLOPs.
questions.explanation: Explanation: Different optimizations change different costs. Structured pruning removes whole channels or blocks, which can reduce actual tensor sizes. Depthwise-separable convolutions replace expensive full convolutions with cheaper spatial and pointwise steps. Distillation trains a smaller student to imitate a stronger teacher. Quantization changes precision, often to integer arithmetic, so floating-point FLOP counts alone cannot describe its benefit. For example, a doorbell camera might use a distilled, quantized student, but only device benchmarks confirm whether its latency and battery use improve.

questions.stem: How should engineers compare FLOPs with accuracy, latency, memory, power, and real-time constraints before deploying an AI model to edge hardware?
options: Compare models using the same inputs and operation-count convention, then benchmark accuracy, p50 and p95 latency, memory use, energy or power, and hardware compatibility. Choose a model that meets deployment limits rather than minimizing FLOPs alone.

Compare estimated FLOPs and test accuracy on the development workstation, then select the smallest operation count. Edge memory, tail latency, and power can be inferred accurately from FLOPs without further measurements.

Rank models primarily by parameter count and batch-average throughput, since these determine battery consumption and real-time reliability. Once training accuracy is sufficient, p95 latency and accelerator compatibility add little meaningful information.

Measure inference latency and FLOPs on the target device, but compare models using different input resolutions when their accuracies differ. Lowering resolution has no effect on fairness because model architecture determines arithmetic independently.
questions.explanation: Explanation: Edge deployment is a trade-off, not a single-number contest. Compare models using identical input resolutions, batch sizes, preprocessing, and FLOP conventions. Then test accuracy, peak memory, energy, and latency on the exact hardware and runtime. For example, a drone object detector may need to finish each frame within a fixed deadline and stay inside a power budget. A lower-FLOP option that misses too many objects or has high p95 latency may be unacceptable. Choose the model that meets all deployment requirements.
